periods.activity_title: Noticing Change — Timescales in Our Lives
periods.textbook_anchor: Changes Around Us — Students think and write about changes noticed in themselves, friends, school, and environment since Grades 3 and 4 (p. 147)

time_bands.activity: The teacher reads aloud the opening story of Saba and Aparna meeting after a year apart and noticing changes in each other. Students share briefly: what is the biggest change they have noticed in themselves or their surroundings recently? The conversation stays concrete and personal — height, hair, a skill learned, a tree that grew.

Students open Textbook p. 147 and write their responses to the task: changes in themselves, friends, school, and environment since Grades 3 and 4. After writing, pairs share one change each. The class then lists examples on the board, and the teacher quietly groups them by how long the change took — without yet naming the categories.

The teacher draws out the groupings explicitly: changes that took many years, changes within a few years, changes that repeat every year, and changes that happen in minutes or seconds. Students revisit their lists and sort their own examples into these four timescales, writing in their notebooks. The teacher prompts with questions — 'Could that happen again? Has it happened before?' — to surface the idea of repeating change.

A brief whole-class share: one student names a change for each timescale while others agree or suggest a better category. The teacher closes by asking students to look around the classroom and name one thing that will look different in ten years — holding the open question without resolving it.

periods.implied_lo: Students can classify observable changes in their environment by the timescale over which they occur and distinguish repeating changes from one-time changes.
periods.section_context: Changes noticed in self and friends since earlier grades, changes in school and environment, long-duration changes, short-duration changes, repeating yearly changes, changes in minutes or seconds, sky colour changes, sun rising and setting.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Can you think of a change that happens again and again, in the same way, at roughly the same time each year?' — this draws out the idea of recurring patterns without giving the word 'season'. Where students mention crops, festivals, or clothing shifts with the weather, welcome these warmly as they carry rich local knowledge worth surfacing.

periods.activity_title: Day and Night — Earth's Rotation Role-Play
periods.section_ref: Changes Around Us in a Day (Day and Night)
periods.textbook_anchor: Changes Around Us in a Day (Day and Night) — Students enact the Sun-Earth rotation role-play and use a torch and globe to show how Earth's rotation causes day and night (p. 150)

time_bands.activity: The teacher asks: 'Does the Sun move around the Earth, or does the Earth move?' Students share initial ideas without correction. The teacher then sets up the role-play described on Textbook p. 150: one student stands at the centre as the Sun, arms outstretched; another student stands a few steps away as the Earth and begins slowly rotating in place, calling out 'day … day …' when facing the Sun and 'night … night …' when facing away.

Three or four student pairs take turns doing the role-play so the experience is shared. After each turn, the teacher asks the watching students: 'What made it change from day to night?' The class arrives together at the idea that the Earth turning — not the Sun moving — causes the change. The teacher introduces the word 'rotation' and writes it on the board.

The teacher dims the room and shines the torch on the globe, holding the torch still while slowly rotating the globe. Students observe which part of the globe is in light and which is in shadow. They then study the globe as directed on Textbook p. 151 and write in their notebooks which countries would have night when India is in daylight, reasoning from what they can see.

Students share their findings aloud. The teacher clarifies that the Sun stays still while the Earth rotates, and briefly mentions the 'Do you know?' note about the globe, seas, and oceans. Students write one sentence in their notebooks: 'Day and night happen because ___.' in their own words.

periods.implied_lo: Students can explain a cyclical natural phenomenon by enacting and observing a physical model and connecting the model's behaviour to the phenomenon's cause.
periods.section_context: Sun-Earth rotation role-play, torch-and-globe demonstration, Earth's axis rotation causing day and night, India's day versus other countries' night, globe features, seas and oceans covering three-fourths of the Earth.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Why do you think people long ago believed the Sun moved across the sky rather than the Earth turning?' — this respects prior folk understanding and opens scientific reasoning. Ensure every student gets at least a moment with the globe in hand so the three-dimensional reality of rotation is felt, not just watched.

periods.activity_title: Seasons' Chart — Building the Wall Chart Together
periods.section_ref: Changes Around Us in a Year (Seasons)
periods.textbook_anchor: Changes Around Us in a Year (Seasons) — Classroom Activity Seasons' Chart Steps 1 and 2: preparing the large wall chart and filling it from class journal observations (p. 152)
materials: Large chart paper or several sheets joined together
Student notebooks with any personal nature observations
periods.visual_aids: Wall-sized Seasons' Chart grid drawn on chart paper (columns: April–June, July–September, October–December, January–March; rows: plant life, birds and animals, air/heat/light, water and water bodies, human activities)

time_bands.activity: The teacher prepares or has students help rule the large grid on chart paper as described on Textbook p. 152: four time-period columns and five theme rows. The teacher reads the column headings and row themes aloud, and students copy the grid structure into their notebooks as a working reference. The teacher explains that the class will fill this chart together from what they have noticed across the year.

Working row by row, the teacher invites students to contribute observations for each theme across each time period. For 'plant life', students describe what they have seen trees, flowers, and crops doing in each period. For 'birds and animals', they share which creatures they notice at different times of year. For 'air/heat/light', 'water and water bodies', and 'human activities', the class contributes together. The teacher or a student scribe writes brief phrases in the relevant cells. Where students differ — because they come from different regions — the teacher notes both and celebrates the variation.

Once the chart is filled, the teacher leads students in scanning across rows and down columns: 'Look at the plant life row — what do you notice from one period to the next? Look at the human activities column for July–September — how does it connect to what is happening in the nature rows?' Students note two or three patterns in their notebooks.
The teacher asks: 'Do you think these patterns will look the same next year? And the year after?' Students respond briefly.

periods.implied_lo: Students can record and organise observations of environmental change across multiple themes and time periods to reveal repeating annual patterns.
periods.section_context: Seasons' Chart grid with time periods April–June, July–September, October–December, January–March, and themes plant life, birds and animals, air/heat/light, water and water bodies, human activities; class journal observations; regional variation in observations.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Has anyone heard a particular bird call or seen a particular flower that tells your family the rains are coming, or the cold is near?' — this invites traditional ecological knowledge organically. If students mention the koel bird or ants carrying eggs to higher ground, treat these as valid observations worthy of the chart, alongside scientific observations.

periods.section_ref: Changes Around Us in a Year (Seasons)
periods.textbook_anchor: Changes Around Us in a Year (Seasons) — Classroom Activity Seasons' Chart Steps 3 and 4: theme-group posters and time-period-group short stories (p. 152)
materials: Completed Seasons' Chart on wall from previous work

time_bands.activity: The teacher quickly re-reads the completed Seasons' Chart with the class and then assigns Step 3 groups as described on Textbook p. 152: five groups of students, each taking one theme row (plant life, birds and animals, air/heat/light, water and water bodies, human activities). Each group's task is to make a poster showing how their theme changes across all four time periods.

Groups work on their posters, drawing and writing key observations from the Seasons' Chart. Each poster should show the four time periods side by side with images or words for their theme. The teacher circulates, asking groups to include at least one example from a different region if the class has students with varied backgrounds, and prompting them to think about what links the changes — 'What is driving plant life to behave this way at this time?'

Each group briefly presents their poster to the class — a quick oral summary, one or two sentences per time period. After all five posters are up, the teacher assigns Step 4 groups: four new groups, each taking one time period (April–June, July–September, October–December, January–March). Each group looks across all five theme posters for their time period and writes a short story linking nature and people's lives in that period.

Groups write their short stories, drawing on observations from the poster display. The teacher encourages them to weave in specific local details — what food is eaten, what work is done, which festivals fall in that period — making the story feel true to their own place.

One group volunteers to read their story aloud. The teacher names what students have just discovered: these repeating patterns across a year are what we call seasons, and introduces the word 'Ritu' along with the six Indian season names.

periods.implied_lo: Students can synthesise multi-theme observations into a creative presentation that connects natural patterns to human cultural life.
periods.section_context: Seasons' Chart Steps 3 and 4, theme-group posters for plant life / birds and animals / air-heat-light / water and water bodies / human activities, time-period short stories, six Indian season names (Vasanta, Grishma, Varsha, Sharad, Hemant, Shishir), Ritu system.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'When your group writes the story for your time period, whose life is changing most — the farmer's, the child's, the trader's? Why?' — this deepens the human-cultural strand. Groups that finish their story quickly can add a title to their poster or sketch a scene from their story.

periods.activity_title: Six Seasons and Regional Patterns — Mapping Our Own Ritu
periods.section_ref: Changes Around Us in a Year (Seasons)
periods.textbook_anchor: Changes Around Us in a Year (Seasons) — Students fill in the months for India's six seasons for their own region using the Ritu table (p. 152)
materials: Completed Seasons' Chart and story-posters on wall
periods.visual_aids: Seasons' Chart and story-posters on wall display

time_bands.activity: The teacher revisits the six season names from the previous unit's closing moment and writes them on the board: Vasanta, Grishma, Varsha, Sharad, Hemant, Shishir. Students draw the six-season table from Textbook p. 152 in their notebooks and discuss, as a class, which months in their region feel like which season. The teacher notes that the months will differ for students from different parts of India.

Students fill in the months column for their own region, then share with a partner to compare. Where two students disagree — because one may be from a coastal area and another from the hills — the teacher treats both as correct for that region and asks the class: 'Why might the same season arrive at different times in different places?' The class discusses briefly, drawing on what they filled in the Seasons' Chart.

The teacher leads a broader discussion connecting the Seasons' Chart observations to the six Ritu names: which cells of the chart belonged to Grishma? Which to Varsha? Students point to the chart and match observations to Ritu names. The teacher brings in the idea that traditional knowledge — like knowing by the koel's call or by ants' behaviour that rain is near — is also a form of reading the seasons, and asks if students know any such signs from their own families.
Students write one sentence in their notebooks: 'In my region, [season name] falls in [months] because ___.' The sentence is their own reasoning, not a copied definition.

periods.implied_lo: Students can identify and explain regional variation in seasonal patterns by connecting personal and local observations to a shared classification system.
periods.section_context: Six Indian season names Vasanta / Grishma / Varsha / Sharad / Hemant / Shishir, student-filled Ritu months table for own region, regional variation in season timing, traditional ecological signs of seasonal change (koel bird, ant behaviour).
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'If a friend from another state filled in the same table, which months do you think would be different? Which might stay the same?' — this keeps the regional diversity discussion concrete. If students share family-transmitted signs of seasonal change, write them on the board alongside the Sanskrit names to validate both registers of knowledge.

periods.activity_title: Seasons and Culture — Crops, Festivals, and Songs
periods.textbook_anchor: Celebrating Seasons — Students name summer and winter crops in their region with help from teachers and elders, and match festivals to their seasons (p. 157)

time_bands.activity: The teacher opens by asking: 'Which festival do you celebrate that feels most connected to the weather or the harvest? Why do you think it falls at that time of year?' Students share freely. The teacher lists festivals named on the board — Pongal/Makar Sankranti, Holi, Diwali, Baisakhi, Gudi Padwa, Vishu, Rongali Bihu — and asks students to call out which season each belongs to, as explored on Textbook p. 157.

Students work in pairs: they open Textbook p. 157 and use the crop task to list summer crops and winter crops known in their region, drawing on what they know from home and elders. Pairs share their lists with the class. The teacher builds a combined board list showing the diversity of crops — some needing the monsoon rains, some needing winter cold, some thriving in summer heat — and connects each crop type back to its season.

The teacher then raises songs: 'Are there songs your family or community sings that belong to a particular season — at harvest, during rains, in spring?' Students share song names or hum fragments. The teacher affirms all contributions and draws out the connection: songs, like festivals and crops, are anchored to the rhythm of the year. The Discuss task from Textbook p. 157 — why winter in Kerala differs from Kashmir, why monsoon differs between Assam and Rajasthan — is posed to the whole class and discussed briefly.

Students write in their notebooks: two crops and one festival associated with any season of their choice, with a one-sentence reason why that season makes those things possible. The teacher collects three or four responses aloud to close the unit.

periods.implied_lo: Students can describe the relationship between seasonal cycles and cultural practices — crops, festivals, and songs — in their own region and compare these with practices from other regions of India.
periods.section_context: Summer crops and winter crops in students' region, festivals linked to seasons (Pongal/Makar Sankranti, Holi, Diwali, Baisakhi, Gudi Padwa, Vishu, Rongali Bihu), season-linked songs, regional differences in winter and monsoon (Kerala vs Kashmir, Assam vs Rajasthan).
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'If the rains failed one year, which festival or crop practice would be most affected in your region? Why?' — this deepens the nature-culture connection and invites empathetic reasoning. Encourage students who come from regions with distinct seasonal traditions to share them as equally valid alongside the textbook examples.

periods.activity_title: My Seasons — Reflecting Through Writing and Drawing
periods.textbook_anchor: Celebrating Seasons — Let us reflect: students fill a table of food, clothes, festivals, and nature for each of the six seasons and make a comparative drawing of three major seasons (p. 160)

time_bands.activity: The teacher briefly recaps what the chapter has explored — changes at different timescales, the cause of day and night, yearly seasonal patterns, and the way seasons shape cultural life — not to summarise the chapter as complete but to give students a starting point for personal reflection. Students open to Textbook p. 160 and read the Let us reflect tasks silently.

Students fill the six-season table on Textbook p. 160: for each of the six seasons, they write the food they eat, clothes they wear, festivals they celebrate, and what nature looks like around them. Students work individually, drawing on personal experience and memory. The teacher circulates and encourages students to use local season names in their own language where they know them, and to name food and festivals specific to their family and region.

Students make a comparative drawing of three major seasons — Summer, Monsoon, and Winter — as described on Textbook p. 160. Each drawing in the trio should show something distinctive: a summer landscape, a monsoon scene, a winter scene, drawn from their own experience of that season. Students add brief labels to each drawing naming one food, one festival, or one nature feature that belongs to that season.

Students share one thing from their table or drawing with a partner — something that surprised them about their own answers, or something they would like to know more about. The teacher closes by acknowledging the diversity visible across the class and naming the big idea: nature's rhythms and human life are woven together, and those rhythms look different from place to place.

periods.implied_lo: Students can express personal and regional experiences of seasonal change through a multi-season comparative drawing and a structured table connecting each season to food, clothing, festivals, and nature.
periods.section_context: Six-season table with food, clothes, festivals, and nature for each season; local season names in regional languages; comparative drawing of Summer, Monsoon, and Winter; personal and family season experiences; regional variation in season experience.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Is there a season your grandparents describe very differently from how you experience it now? What might explain that difference?' — this opens awareness of climate change without prescribing a conclusion. Students who find writing difficult may draw all three panels first and label them, letting the drawing carry the meaning.

assessment_items.question_text: Saba notices that the leaves on the neem tree outside her house fall off every year and then grow back. What kind of change does this best describe?

options.label: A
options.text: A change that happens once and never reverses.

options.label: B
options.text: A change that happens within a few minutes.

options.label: C
options.text: A change that repeats again and again on a yearly cycle.

options.label: D
options.text: A change that takes many decades to complete.

assessment_items.annotation: The correct answer is C. This item checks whether students can classify a repeating yearly change correctly within the four-timescale framework built during the unit.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can classify observable changes in their environment by the timescale over which they occur and distinguish repeating changes from one-time changes.

competency.competency_text: Asks questions and makes predictions about simple patterns (season change, food chain, phases of the moon, movement of stars and planets, shapes of trees, plants, leaves, and flowers, rituals, celebrations) observed in the immediate environment

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student confuses a reversible repeating change with a permanent one-time change — they have not grasped the cyclical nature of leaf fall and regrowth.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student associates natural change with a very long timescale (decades), conflating this yearly repeating change with slow geological or growth changes discussed in the same section.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student selects the fastest timescale discussed in the unit — a minutes-or-seconds change — suggesting they have not linked the annual leaf cycle to the yearly-repeating category.

assessment_items.question_text: In the Sun-Earth role-play, one student played the Sun and another played Earth. The student playing Earth slowly turned around (rotated). Write two things this activity showed about why day and night happen.
expected_elements: The Earth rotates (turns on its own axis) — not the Sun moving — to create day and night.
The side of the Earth facing the Sun experiences day; the side facing away experiences night.
As the Earth rotates, each part of it moves from day into night and back again in a cycle.
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any two of the three expected elements for full credit. A response that says 'the Sun moves around the Earth' without correction indicates a persistent misconception to address.
assessment_items.chapter_section: Changes Around Us in a Day (Day and Night)
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can explain a cyclical natural phenomenon by enacting and observing a physical model and connecting the model's behaviour to the phenomenon's cause.

competency.competency_text: Gains familiarity with disciplinary core ideas in the natural sciences, as well as in engineering, technology, and applications of science, which reflect the content that will be learned across subject areas in later Grades

expected_elements: The Earth rotates (turns on its own axis) — not the Sun moving — to create day and night.
The side of the Earth facing the Sun experiences day; the side facing away experiences night.
As the Earth rotates, each part of it moves from day into night and back again in a cycle.

assessment_items.question_text: The class made a Seasons' Chart with rows for plant life, birds and animals, air/heat/light, water and water bodies, and human activities. Which of the following BEST explains why the chart had four time-period columns?

options.label: A
options.text: To divide the year into periods when nature and human activities change in recognisable ways that repeat every year.

options.label: B
options.text: To list the four days of the week when the most changes happen.

options.label: C
options.text: To show that changes happen only four times in a lifetime.

options.label: D
options.text: To show the four directions — North, South, East, and West — in which seasons travel.

assessment_items.annotation: The correct answer is B. This item checks whether students understand the structural purpose of the chart — to reveal repeating annual patterns across time periods.
assessment_items.chapter_section: Changes Around Us in a Year (Seasons)
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can record and organise observations of environmental change across multiple themes and time periods to reveal repeating annual patterns.

competency.competency_text: Identifies natural and humanmade systems that support their lives (water supply, water cycle, river flow systems, seasons, life cycle of plants and animals, food, household items, transport, communication, electricity in the home)

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student misreads the four columns as representing four events in a lifetime — they have not connected the columns to the yearly repeating cycle that the chart was designed to reveal.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student confuses the organisational concept of time periods with a spatial/directional concept, suggesting they have not engaged with the chart's logic.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student reduces the chart's time periods to days of the week, indicating a failure to grasp that the columns represent months-long periods within a year.

assessment_items.task: Choose ONE of the five themes from the Seasons' Chart — plant life, birds and animals, air/heat/light, water and water bodies, or human activities. Make a poster showing how your chosen theme changes across all four time periods of the year (April–June, July–September, October–December, January–March). Use drawings, labels, and a few sentences to show what happens in each period. At the bottom of your poster, write ONE sentence saying what you notice about the overall pattern.
assessment_items.scaffold:
My theme: ___
April–June: [drawing + 1–2 labels]
July–September: [drawing + 1–2 labels]
October–December: [drawing + 1–2 labels]
January–March: [drawing + 1–2 labels]
Overall pattern I notice: ___
format_of_output: Poster with drawings and labels for each of the four time periods
One summary sentence naming the overall pattern
assessment_items.annotation: Assess whether the student shows change across all four periods for their chosen theme and identifies a repeating pattern. A strong poster will show variation across periods, not the same image four times. Regionally varied content (e.g., different crops, different birds) is correct and should be credited fully.
assessment_items.chapter_section: Changes Around Us in a Year (Seasons)
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can synthesise multi-theme observations into a creative presentation that connects natural patterns to human cultural life.

competency.competency_text: Presents observations and findings through different creative modes (drawing, diagram, poem, play, skit, oral and written expression)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student can organise seasonal observations for a specific theme into a visual format that shows change over time and identify the repeating pattern underlying those changes.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: Check that all four time periods are addressed and are visually or textually distinct. The summary sentence is the key analytic moment — it should name a pattern, not just repeat an observation.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: clear differentiation across all four periods with accurate local detail; summary sentence names a cyclical pattern (e.g., 'rains bring growth and then the dry months bring harvest'). Weak: the same image repeated for multiple periods, or a summary sentence that merely describes one period rather than the overall pattern.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who find drawing difficult may use written labels alone; students who find writing difficult may use drawings with minimal labels. Both pathways reach the same analytical outcome.
OPEN_TASK.format_type: Poster with drawings and written labels
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: A poster integrates visual and written modes, matching the Seasons' Chart activity from which this task directly grows, and allows students to demonstrate synthesis across time periods concretely.

assessment_items.question_text: Priya lives in a hilly region and her friend Meena lives on the coast. When Priya fills in the Ritu table, she writes that Hemant (pre-winter) falls in October and November. Meena writes different months for the same season. Write two reasons why their tables might show different months for the same Indian season.
expected_elements: India is a large country with different geographical features — hills, coasts, plains, deserts — that experience temperature and rainfall differently.
The same season (e.g., Hemant/pre-winter) arrives earlier or later and feels more or less intense depending on altitude, distance from the sea, and local climate.
Regional variation means the months that feel cold or rainy differ from place to place, so the same Ritu name maps to different calendar months in different regions.
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any two distinct reasons that reference regional or geographical difference. Responses that mention only that 'everyone is different' without naming a geographical or climatic reason are partial — prompt the student to say why the regions differ. Regionally specific examples (e.g., coastal humidity, hill altitude) are correct and should be credited.
assessment_items.chapter_section: Changes Around Us in a Year (Seasons)
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can identify and explain regional variation in seasonal patterns by connecting personal and local observations to a shared classification system.

competency.competency_text: Asks questions and makes predictions about simple patterns (season change, food chain, phases of the moon, movement of stars and planets, shapes of trees, plants, leaves, and flowers, rituals, celebrations) observed in the immediate environment

expected_elements: India is a large country with different geographical features — hills, coasts, plains, deserts — that experience temperature and rainfall differently.
The same season (e.g., Hemant/pre-winter) arrives earlier or later and feels more or less intense depending on altitude, distance from the sea, and local climate.
Regional variation means the months that feel cold or rainy differ from place to place, so the same Ritu name maps to different calendar months in different regions.

assessment_items.question_text: Baisakhi is celebrated in Punjab at the time of the wheat harvest. Rongali Bihu is celebrated in Assam at the start of the agricultural new year. Pongal is celebrated in Tamil Nadu after the rice harvest. What does the timing of these three festivals tell us about the relationship between seasons, crops, and celebrations in India? Give reasons for your answer.
look_for: The student recognises that all three festivals are timed to mark a key moment in the agricultural/seasonal calendar — harvest, planting season, or seasonal transition.
The student identifies that different crops (wheat, rice) grow in different seasons and regions, so the festivals celebrating them fall at different times of year.
The student makes a general claim: seasons shape when crops are ready, and crops shape when festivals are held — nature and culture are linked in a cycle.
A strong response uses at least two of the three festivals as evidence and draws a conclusion that goes beyond describing each festival separately.
assessment_items.annotation: This item invites a reasoned argument, not a list. Award credit for the quality of the connection made between seasons, crops, and celebrations rather than for naming additional festivals. Regionally specific additional examples from the student's own background are valid evidence and should be credited fully.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can describe the relationship between seasonal cycles and cultural practices — crops, festivals, and songs — in their own region and compare these with practices from other regions of India.

competency.competency_text: Describes the relationship between the natural environment and cultural practices in their immediate environment (nature of work, food, festivals, traditions)

assessment_items.task: Make a comparative drawing of three seasons — Summer, Monsoon, and Winter — as you experience them in your region. For each season, draw a scene that shows what the land, plants, sky, and people look like. Below each drawing, complete these sentences: 'In [season], I eat ___ and wear ___. The festival I celebrate is ___. Nature around me looks like ___.'
assessment_items.scaffold: Summer drawing → 'In Summer, I eat ___ and wear ___. The festival I celebrate is ___. Nature around me looks like ___.' | Monsoon drawing → 'In Monsoon, I eat ___ and wear ___. The festival I celebrate is ___. Nature around me looks like ___.' | Winter drawing → 'In Winter, I eat ___ and wear ___. The festival I celebrate is ___. Nature around me looks like ___.'
format_of_output: Three drawings, one per season, each showing land, plants, sky, and people
Three completed sentence sets, one below each drawing
assessment_items.annotation: Assess whether each drawing and sentence set is distinct and reflects genuine seasonal difference as experienced by the student. There is no single correct answer — food, clothing, festivals, and nature will all vary by region and community. Regionally varied responses are fully correct. A strong response shows clear differences across the three seasons; a weak one repeats similar details for two or more seasons.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can express personal and regional experiences of seasonal change through a multi-season comparative drawing and a structured table connecting each season to food, clothing, festivals, and nature.

competency.competency_text: Observes and describes cultural diversity in their immediate environment (food, clothing, games, different seasons, festivals related to harvest and sowing)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student can draw on personal and regional experience to represent three distinct seasons visually and linguistically, connecting each to food, clothing, festivals, and nature — demonstrating awareness of cultural diversity shaped by seasonal cycles.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: Check that all three drawings are visually distinct and that the sentence sets below each are specific rather than generic. 'Nature around me looks like ___' is the richest prompt — it should show something particular to that season, not a blank or generic landscape.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: three clearly differentiated drawings with specific local food, clothing, a named festival, and a distinctive nature description for each. Weak: two or more drawings look nearly identical, or the sentence sets repeat the same food/festival/clothing across seasons.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who find drawing difficult may focus on detailed sentence sets with simple sketch outlines. Students who find writing difficult may use drawing as the primary carrier with single-word labels. Both reach the same demonstrable outcome.
OPEN_TASK.format_type: Comparative drawing triptych with sentence labels
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: Drawing is an explicit creative mode in C-6.2 and is the textbook's own closing task for this chapter, making it the most authentic and accessible format for demonstrating personal seasonal experience.
